en.title: Street Fighter Movie Director Explains Its "Gonzo" Action Style
en.summary: Director Kitao Sakurai reveals the intentional choice to embrace over-the-top absurdity and silliness for the new Street Fighter movie. The film leans into a "gonzo" energy, drawing inspiration from unconventional comedy.
en.body:
Forget gritty realism and grounded fight choreography; the new **Street Fighter** movie is leaning hard into a wild, over-the-top, and decidedly "gonzo" style. Director **Kitao Sakurai** recently shared his vision for the film, explaining that the goal was to capture a unique energy that embraces absurdity and silliness, a stark contrast to the more grounded approaches seen in many other video game adaptations.

Sakurai, known for his work on the wonderfully chaotic **The Eric Andre Show**, stated that he intentionally infused the **Street Fighter** movie with a similar spirit. "There’s a silliness to it, and there’s an absurdity to the world and the characters and how they interact," he told The Hollywood Reporter. He emphasized that while not every moment needs to be a laugh-out-loud gag, "every minute needs to be interesting." This philosophy allows for elements that might not make perfect narrative sense but contribute to the film's overall frenetic energy and unique feeling.

## A "Gonzo" Vision for Shadaloo

Producer **Cale Boyter** at Legendary was instrumental in championing this particular vision for **Street Fighter**, one that embraces a "gonzo energy." This approach, reminiscent of the unconventional and often absurd nature described in contexts like the Burning Man Project, suggests a deliberate move away from predictable action tropes. The film aims to be unpredictable, mirroring the wild special moves and vibrant personalities that fans have loved in the games for decades.

Sakurai also highlighted the importance of bringing the original directors of the 1994 **Street Fighter** film, the Philippou brothers, back for cameo roles. His personal invitation for them to appear as two people fighting in the street was a deliberate message: "There's no bad blood. We're all part of the same family. There was no animosity, and it’s all love.” This gesture underscores the film's intention to celebrate the franchise's legacy rather than distance itself from past interpretations.

## What This Means for Fans

For **Street Fighter** fans, Sakurai's "gonzo" approach is a welcome sign that the movie isn't afraid to have fun. While the film's box office performance so far has been modest, its commitment to a unique, high-energy style could resonate with audiences tired of formulaic action flicks. It suggests a willingness to capture the spirit of the games, which are known for their colorful characters and over-the-top special attacks, rather than attempting to force them into a hyper-realistic mold.

## Looking Ahead

With **Noah Centineo** as Ken, **Callina Liang** as Chun-Li, and **Andrew Koji** as Ryu, the film has assembled a cast ready to embody its energetic tone. While the current worldwide gross stands at over $55 million, the director's clear artistic intent offers a compelling reason for fans to experience this *different* take on the iconic fighting game franchise.

I also love comedy and craziness and energy," he told The Hollywood Reporter . Also in the interview, Sakurai discussed how his work on The Eric Andre Show informed his filmmaking sensibilities for Street Fighter. He said he learned from that show that not every minute needs to be hilarious, but "every minute needs to be interesting." "So there can be elements that are so ridiculous they might not track narratively or make sense conceptually, but because they’re part of an overall energy and feeling, they fit. So I kept that in mind when I was developing this film," he said. Also in the interview, Sakurai talked about how Street Fighter's original movie directors, the Philippou brothers, ended up appearing in cameo roles. He said he personally invited them to appear in the movie as two people ... fighting in the street. Sakurai said he wanted the Australian brothers to be in the movie as a means to communicate how, "There's no bad blood. We're all part of the same family." "There was no animosity, and it’s all love,” Sakurai said. The Street Fighter movie hit theaters on October 16, and it's made more than $55 million worldwide so far , and that's not so great . The movie stars Noah Centineo as Ken, Callina Liang as Chun-Li, Andrew Koji as Ryu, Jason Momoa as Blanka, Cody Rhodes as Guile, Roman Reigns as Akuma, and David Dastmalchian as M. Bison.
